newsitem.title: USA: US considers collecting data on mixed races.
newsitem.headline: US considers collecting data on mixed races.

text.p: Several federal agencies recommended Tuesday that Americans of mixed race be able to reflect that on census forms and other government reports.

A 150-page report by an interagency task force recommended unanimously that federal data collection forms including the 2000 census be changed so people can check off one or more racial identifications.
"I would not underestimate the effect of that change," Sally Katzen, head of the Office of Management and Budget's information and regulatory affairs office, said.

"The way the numbers will be assembled and reported will be very significant in that we will be providing numbers on those people with mixed racial heritages by categories in the aggregate and individual combinations of those."

The recommendations were made by a 30-agency task force and were subject to a 60-day public review and comment period before OMB decides whether to accept them, Katzen said. The report was to be published in Wednesday's Federal Register, the government's regulatory publication.

The proposed change was meant to reflect a small but growing portion of the population. If it is adopted, someone like champion golfer Tiger Woods, for example, could check both Asian and African American on the 2000 census form.

The interagency group, which has been examining and testing the collection of racial data for years, rejected creating a new category called "multiracial," saying it would not provide useful information but would add to racial tensions and further fragmentation of the population.

Katzen said the 1990 census used the term "other" in the racial categories and nearly 10 million people checked that. But she said it created some confusion and would be dropped if the proposed changes were accepted.

The design of the racial data collected has not changed since 1977 when the orginal OMB directive was issued to set racial data collection standards for agencies that needed the information to enforce the nation's civil rights laws.

"The category set forth in the directive in 1977 reflected our political and social determinations," Katzen said. "They were not anthropologically based, they were not scientifically based. It was a political social construct that was used."

The agencies recommended no new racial or ethnic categories be added to the four -- Black, White, American Indian or Alaskan native, and Asian or Pacific Islander -- that have been in use for the last 20 years. But the census would gather information on the ancestry of population groups.

They recommended that questions about the U.S. Hispanic population be kept separate from racial categories and be asked before the racial question. The report said testing showed that this format produced more complete data on Hispanics, who often checked "other" in the racial category or failed to respond to the race question if it was asked before questions about ethnic origins.

The group also recommended that the "Black" category be changed to say "Black or African American" and that the term "American Indian" should not be changed to "native American." It recommended that the term "Hawaiian" be changed to "native Hawaiian."
The group suggested the changes be used in the 2000 census and that all other federal data collection conform by 2003.
